---
title: Connect a web page
description: Let a page in a browser register itself with an instance, get the owner's approval in a small window, and read the owner's data with the token it receives.
---

A web page connects the way any [app connects with OAuth](/build/authenticate#connect-an-app-with-oauth), with every step taken by the page's own script. The instance needs no setup and the page holds no key. The page registers itself, the owner approves it once, and from then on the instance answers the page's address from a browser. The example is a photo frame page that shows the owner's pictures.

## What the page needs

- **An `https` address with a real host name.** A page registers as a web client, whose redirect addresses must be `https` and off the loopback, so a page served from `http://localhost` can't connect this way.
- **A callback page** at the redirect address, which hands the code back to the page. The callback step shows it.
- **An instance the browser can reach.** When a page on a public address calls an instance on a private or loopback address, Chrome asks the person for local network access first, and blocks the request if they decline.

## Connect the page

<Steps>
<Step>

### Find the endpoints

The discovery document answers any origin with no credential, so a page that isn't approved yet can read it:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const instance = "https://marfa.example.com";

const meta = await (
  await fetch(`${instance}/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`)
).json();
// meta.registration_endpoint, meta.authorization_endpoint, meta.token_endpoint
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Register the page

Registration also takes no credential and answers any origin. Name the page's callback address, whose origin is the one the owner approves:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const redirectUri = `${location.origin}/callback`;
const scope = "core.file.image:read";

const registered = await (
  await fetch(meta.registration_endpoint, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      client_name: "Photo frame",
      redirect_uris: [redirectUri],
      scope,
    }),
  })
).json();
const clientId: string = registered.client_id;
```

Marfa answers `201` with the `client_id`. A page keeps no secret, and Marfa registers every client as public, proving itself with PKCE. Name the scopes: without `scope`, a registration asks for read and write on everything.

A registration nobody approves is removed after an hour idle, the `unapproved_app_retention_hours` [setting](/run/settings). Register again at each connection until the owner approves, then keep the `client_id`.

</Step>
<Step>

### Make the PKCE pair and a state

Marfa accepts only PKCE with `S256`. Make a random verifier, its challenge, and a `state` of your own:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const base64url = (bytes: ArrayBuffer | Uint8Array) =>
  btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new Uint8Array(bytes)))
    .replace(/\+/g, "-")
    .replace(/\//g, "_")
    .replace(/=+$/, "");

const random = (size: number) => base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(size)));
const verifier = random(32);
const state = random(16);
const challenge = base64url(
  await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)),
);
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Open the approval window

Listen for the answer first, because it can arrive before the next line returns. Every tab of the page hears every callback, so keep only the answer with this connection's `state`. Then open the authorization endpoint in a small window, from a click, because browsers block a window no click opened:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const answered = new Promise<URLSearchParams>((resolve) => {
  const channel = new BroadcastChannel("marfa-approval");
  channel.onmessage = (event) => {
    const answer = new URLSearchParams(event.data);
    if (answer.get("state") !== state) return;
    channel.close();
    resolve(answer);
  };
});

const authorize = new URL(meta.authorization_endpoint);
authorize.search = new URLSearchParams({
  response_type: "code",
  client_id: clientId,
  redirect_uri: redirectUri,
  scope,
  state,
  code_challenge: challenge,
  code_challenge_method: "S256",
}).toString();
open(authorize, "marfa-approval", "popup,width=480,height=640");
```

The window asks the owner to sign in if needed. It then shows the page's name with a caution that Marfa can't confirm who made it, **the page's host**, and a choice between **Full access**, which grants everything the page asks for, and **Choose access**, which lets the owner give less. [Approve an app](/run/manage-apps#approve-an-app) describes the choices.

</Step>
<Step>

### Hand the code back from the callback page

When the owner decides, Marfa sends the window to the callback address with `code`, `state` and `iss`, or with `error=access_denied` if the owner denied the page. The callback page runs at the page's own origin, so it passes the result over a `BroadcastChannel`, which only that origin hears, and closes:

```html title="callback.html"
<!doctype html>
<title>Connecting</title>
<script>
  new BroadcastChannel("marfa-approval").postMessage(location.search);
  close();
</script>
```

The main page waits on the channel it opened, and checks the answer:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const answer = await answered;

if (answer.get("error")) throw new Error(`not approved: ${answer.get("error")}`);
if (answer.get("iss") !== meta.issuer) throw new Error("answer from another server");
const code = answer.get("code")!;
```

An owner who closes the window sends nothing, so give the page a way to cancel the wait.

</Step>
<Step>

### Exchange the code

Send the code and the verifier to the token endpoint as a form:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const token = await (
  await fetch(meta.token_endpoint, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
    body: new URLSearchParams({
      grant_type: "authorization_code",
      code,
      redirect_uri: redirectUri,
      client_id: clientId,
      code_verifier: verifier,
    }),
  })
).json();
```

```json title="Response" status="200"
{
  "access_token": "marfa_at_…",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "scope": "core.file.image:read"
}
```

A code works once. `scope` lists what the owner chose, which can be less than the page asked for.

</Step>
<Step>

### Read the owner's data

Send the access token in the `Authorization` header:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const response = await fetch(`${instance}/items?type=core.file.image&limit=20`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token.access_token}` },
});
const { data: pictures, next_cursor } = await response.json();
```

Don't send `credentials: "include"`: Marfa never allows credentials on a cross-origin answer, so the page works only with the token it holds. [List, filter and search](/build/list-filter-search) covers the listing.

The token expires after `expires_in` seconds. To get another, open the approval window again and exchange the new code: an owner who is signed in and already approved these scopes goes straight back with a code. To disconnect, [revoke access](/build/authenticate#revoke-access).

</Step>
</Steps>

## Redirect the whole page instead

For a browser that blocks windows, skip the window and send the browser itself to the authorization address. The callback address is then the page itself. Before leaving, keep the `verifier`, `state` and `client_id` in `sessionStorage`. On return, read `code`, `state` and `iss` from the query string, check them, then exchange the code.

## What the approval allows

Approving the page lets the origin (scheme, host and port) of each redirect address it registered call the instance from a browser, until the last app approved on that origin is disconnected. Before approval, only discovery and registration answer the page.

**The access token is the only authority.** The origin lets the browser deliver answers to the page, and gives it nothing else.

An owner who trusts an origin in advance names it in the `cors_origins` setting:

```bash
marfa config set cors_origins https://frame.example.com
```

A native app's redirect address allows no origin, because it is where a program on a device listens, not a page.

## If a step fails

| What the page sees | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Registration answers `413 request_too_large` | The body is over 8 KiB. |
| Registration answers `400 invalid_redirect_uri` | An address isn't `https`, is on the loopback, doesn't parse, or the registration names more than 10. |
| The code never reaches the page | The callback page is missing, or posts on a channel of another name. |
| A request is blocked with no response | The owner hasn't approved the page, denied it or disconnected it, or the page's origin isn't the origin of a redirect address it registered. |
| The token endpoint answers `400 invalid_grant` | The code was used already, or the verifier doesn't match its challenge. |

The rules behind this guide are in the [keys and sign-in](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/keys-and-oauth.md#web-pages) chapter of the contract.
